Project: /workspace — two C++ compiler-lab front-end tools that were just finished.
  /workspace/LexicalAnalyzer/LexicalAnalysis.cpp   (lexer, complete)
  /workspace/Parser/SyntacticParser.cpp            (LL(1) parser, complete)
  /workspace/requirements/*.yaml                   (27 requirements, one per module)
  /workspace/agent_tests/run_lex.sh                (builds+runs the lexer in a scratch dir)
  /workspace/agent_tests/run_parser.sh <grammar> <input>  (builds+runs the parser; grammar copied to test3.txt, input piped on stdin)
  /workspace/agent_tests/test_parser_units.cpp     (unit tests: g++ -std=c++11 -Wall -o /tmp/pu agent_tests/test_parser_units.cpp && /tmp/pu)
  /workspace/LexicalAnalyzer/processed.txt and afterPreProcess.txt are GBK-encoded REFERENCE outputs from the original author — the lexer must reproduce them (modulo the UTF-8 vs GBK width of Chinese header text).

Grammars: test1 "E::=a|b|(T)  T::=EG  G::=,EG|@"   test2 "E::=AB|a  A::=C|bDA  B::=@  C::=cAD|@  D::=dBe"   test3 "E::=aH  H::=aMd|d  M::=Ab|@  A::=aM|e".
'@' = epsilon, '#' = end marker. Hidden grader tests compile and run the binaries and depend on these exact entry points (signatures must not drift):
  preProcess, mainProcess, IsIdentifier, IsNum, wtMatch, findError,
  load_file, split_into_rules, operator<<(rule), check_rules, check_set,
  operator<<(F_set), findFirst, checkFirst, findFollow, checkFollow,
  LL_1, operator<<(LL_1_table), print_state, syntacticAnalysis.

YOU MAY RUN the build/test commands above (read-only w.r.t. the repo: build into /tmp, never edit repo files, never run git write commands). Actually execute things — do not speculate. Report only defects you can demonstrate.


A prior auditor reported this finding:
{
  "title": "is_non_terminal() only scans rule left-hand sides, so an uppercase symbol used in a right part but never defined is printed as a member of a FIRST set",
  "file": "/workspace/Parser/SyntacticParser.cpp",
  "line": 258,
  "severity": "nit",
  "repro": "mkdir -p /tmp/x5 && printf 'S::=Xa|b\\n' > /tmp/x5/test3.txt && g++ -std=c++11 -Wall -o /tmp/x5/parser /workspace/Parser/SyntacticParser.cpp && cd /tmp/x5 && printf 'b\\n' | ./parser\n\nObserved output:\n  各规则右部的First集：\n      First(Xa)={X}          <- X reported as a terminal in a FIRST set\n      First(b)={b}\n  各非终结符的Follow集：\n      Follow(S)={#}\n      Follow(X)={#,a}        <- ...and as a non-terminal two lines later\n\nExpected: First(Xa)={} (X has no production, so it derives nothing). The verdicts are still right (X gets no column, the cell stays empty and 'b' is accepted / 'xa' rejected) — this is a reporting inconsistency only. split_into_rules line 198 and the row-header loop at line 401 both classify RHS-only uppercase symbols as non-terminals, but is_non_terminal() at line 258 only looks at rules[i].left, so firstOf() falls through to the terminal branch and inserts 'X' into the FIRST set.",
  "fix": "Give firstOf a non-terminal test consistent with the rest of the program — either pass the non_terminal set down, or extend the check:\n\n    static bool is_non_terminal(const char c, const vector<rule>& rules) {\n        for (unsigned int i = 0; i < rules.size(); i++)\n            if (rules[i].left == c) return true;\n        return isupper((unsigned char)c) != 0;   // 只出现在右部的大写字母同样是非终结符\n    }\n\nWith that, a non-terminal with no production contributes nothing to FIRST (the alternative loop finds no rules, has_epsilon stays false, all_epsilon is cleared) and First(Xa) prints as {}."
}

You are a SKEPTIC. Try to REFUTE it: reproduce it yourself with the commands given. If it does not reproduce, or it is cosmetic/expected behaviour (e.g. UTF-8 vs GBK setw width, trailing spaces from setw padding, Chinese text alignment), mark isReal=false. Default to isReal=false when uncertain.

#!/bin/sh
# Build and run the LL(1) parser inside a scratch directory.
#
# Usage: agent_tests/run_parser.sh <grammar-file> <input-string> [scratch_dir]
#   e.g. agent_tests/run_parser.sh test3.txt aaabd
set -e
ROOT=$(cd "$(dirname "$0")/.." && pwd)
GRAMMAR=${1:-test3.txt}
INPUT=${2:-aaabd}
WORK=${3:-/tmp/parser_run}

rm -rf "$WORK"
mkdir -p "$WORK"
cp "$ROOT"/Parser/test*.txt "$WORK/"
# main() hard-codes ./test3.txt, so present the requested grammar under that name.
# (copying test3.txt onto itself is an error, so skip that case)
if [ "$GRAMMAR" != "test3.txt" ]; then
	cp "$WORK/$GRAMMAR" "$WORK/test3.txt"
fi
g++ -std=c++11 -Wall -o "$WORK/parser" "$ROOT/Parser/SyntacticParser.cpp"

cd "$WORK"
printf '%s\n' "$INPUT" | ./parser
echo ""

content.text:
Comprehensively verified. Here is my assessment.

**The output reproduces exactly** — `printf 'S::=Xa|b\n'` does print `First(Xa)={X}` while listing `X` under 非终结符 (not 终结符) and giving it a `Follow(X)` line. So the auditor's observation is factually accurate, and there is a genuine convention mismatch: `split_into_rules` (line ~198) and the `LL_1` row-header loop (line ~403, whose own comment reads "只出现在右部、没有产生式的非终结符同样占一行") classify RHS-only uppercase letters as non-terminals, while `is_non_terminal()` at line 258 only scans `rules[i].left`.

**But it is print-only, on out-of-spec input, with provably zero functional impact.** I built the auditor's own suggested patch (`return isupper((unsigned char)c) != 0;`) into `/tmp/fix/patched.cpp` and diffed it against the shipped binary:

- All three official grammars (`test1`/`test2`/`test3`) × 7 inputs each: **21/21 byte-identical output**. Every uppercase symbol in those grammars has a production, so the branch is never reached.
- Degenerate grammars (`S::=Xa|b`, `S::=AXb A::=c|@`, `S::=Xa|b T::=Xc`): the **only** lines that differ are the `First(...)` / `Follow(...)` echo lines. The `LL(1)分析表` is byte-identical and every accept/reject verdict is identical.

The reason is structural, not luck: the spurious symbol is always an uppercase char that lives in `non_terminal` and never in `terminal`, so it can never match a table column and is always skipped by the `col_it == table.col.end() → continue` guard. The epsilon bookkeeping is also unchanged — both the buggy path (terminal branch: `all_epsilon=false; break`) and the fixed path (non-terminal with no matching rules: `has_epsilon` stays false → `all_epsilon=false; break`) terminate identically. The only delta is the extra `result.insert(c)`.

No requirement covers undefined non-terminals — `parser_first_core.yaml` and `parser_rule_parser.yaml` specify only signatures and normal FIRST/epsilon semantics. `test_parser_units.cpp` passes 59/59 and contains no case for this. The named entry points are untouched either way.

The auditor themselves grade it `severity: nit` and write "this is a reporting inconsistency only." That is the correct characterization, and it puts it in the same discount bucket as the formatting artifacts: a display-layer quirk reachable only by a malformed grammar, with no behavioral consequence.

Relevant files: `/workspace/Parser/SyntacticParser.cpp` (`is_non_terminal` line 258, `firstOf` line 290, `LL_1` row loop line 403), `/workspace/agent_tests/test_parser_units.cpp`.

I built the auditor's own suggested patch (is_non_terminal returning isupper(c) as a fallback) as /tmp/fix/patched.cpp and diffed shipped vs patched:
  - test1/test2/test3 x 7 inputs each: 21/21 byte-identical output.
  - Degenerate grammars ('S::=Xa|b', 'S::=AXb    A::=c|@', 'S::=Xa|b    T::=Xc') x 4 inputs each: the ONLY differing lines are the First(...)/Follow(...) echo lines. The LL(1)分析表 block is byte-identical and every accept/reject verdict ("...是/不是该文法的句子") is identical.

input.reasoning:
The observation reproduces literally, and there is a real convention mismatch inside the file (split_into_rules line ~198 and the LL_1 row-header loop line ~403 treat RHS-only uppercase letters as non-terminals, while is_non_terminal at line 258 only scans rules[i].left). But it fails the bar for a reportable defect on three independent grounds, each demonstrated rather than argued.

1. Zero functional impact, verified by differential testing. I compiled the auditor's own proposed fix and compared it against the shipped binary. On all three specified grammars the output is byte-identical across 21 runs, because every uppercase symbol in test1/test2/test3 has a production so the divergent branch is never reached. On deliberately malformed grammars the only lines that change are the First(...)/Follow(...) echo lines; the LL(1) table renders byte-identically and every accept/reject verdict is unchanged.

2. The invariance is structural, not coincidental. The spuriously inserted symbol is always an uppercase char that is placed in non_terminal and never in terminal, so it can never match a table column and is always dropped by the "col_it == table.col.end() -> continue" guard when filling cells. The epsilon bookkeeping is also identical on both paths: the terminal branch does all_epsilon=false then break, and the fixed non-terminal branch finds no matching rules so has_epsilon stays false, giving all_epsilon=false then break. The sole behavioral delta is one extra result.insert(c) that nothing downstream can consume.

3. It is only reachable via out-of-spec input. It requires a grammar containing an uppercase symbol used in a right part with no production at all - an ill-formed grammar. The three assignment grammars (test1, test2, test3) all define every uppercase symbol they use, so no grader run over them can observe this. No requirement covers undefined non-terminals: parser_first_core.yaml and parser_rule_parser.yaml specify only the entry-point signatures plus ordinary FIRST/epsilon semantics. test_parser_units.cpp passes 59/59 and has no case for it. None of the protected entry-point signatures are implicated either way.

The auditor grades this "nit" and concedes in their own repro text that "the verdicts are still right ... this is a reporting inconsistency only." That self-assessment is accurate and places it squarely in the cosmetic/display bucket the task instructs me to discount, alongside setw padding and encoding-width artifacts: a text-formatting quirk on malformed input with no consequence for the analysis table, the parse trace, or the final verdict.
